a: The LORD's word came to me:
p: Chapters 16 to 19 carry no date of their own; their place in the book points to about 592 to 591 BC.
b: Ezekiel dates his visions from the exile of King Jehoiachin in 597 BC. The last date before this part is 8:1, the sixth year (592 BC), and the next is 20:1, the seventh year (591 BC). The chapters between them are usually read as belonging to that stretch. Chapter 17 reports a revolt against Babylon (17:15), and some scholars think that part was spoken a little later, as Zedekiah's plotting grew. The Plain gives the dates as the book's frame and does not claim more. All these chapters were first heard by the exiles who gathered at Ezekiel's house in Babylon (8:1; 14:1; 20:1).

a: make Jerusalem know
t: A trial speech, and a rule for reading it aloud
p: Hoda' means 'make known', as in a court. The rabbis would not let this chapter be read in the synagogue as a prophetic reading.
b: Hoda' is the verb of a prosecutor laying out charges, and the chapter is built like a court case (compare 20:4; 22:2). The Mishnah records that Rabbi Eliezer said 'Make Jerusalem know her abhorrent things' is not to be read as the prophetic reading (Mishnah Megillah 4:10), and the Talmud tells of a man who read it before him and was told to go and look into his own mother's abhorrent things (Babylonian Talmud, Megillah 25b). The reason is the chapter's frank language and its picture of Israel's shame. Other sages did not ban it, and it has a place in later synagogue practice.

a: abhorrent things
p: To'evah is the Bible's strong word for what God cannot bear, and Ezekiel uses it far more than any other prophet.
b: To'evah names things that are an offense to God, such as idol worship (Deuteronomy 7:25), child sacrifice (Deuteronomy 12:31) and sexual wrongs (Leviticus 18). Ezekiel uses the plural again and again (5:9; 6:9; 7:3; 8:6, and in this chapter at 16:22, 36, 43, 47, 51, 58). The Plain says 'abhorrent things' every time, so a reader can follow the word through the book. It is not the same word as gillulim, 'filthy idols' (see 16:36), or shiqqutsim, 'detestable things'.

a: Your father was Amorite, your mother Hittite.
p: Jerusalem was a Canaanite city before David took it. Ezekiel turns that fact into an insult.
b: Before David, Jerusalem belonged to the Jebusites (Joshua 15:63; 2 Samuel 5:6–9). 'Amorite' and 'Hittite' are two of the old names for the peoples of Canaan before Israel (Genesis 15:16–21; Genesis 10:15–16). Ezekiel is not giving a family record. He is saying that the city had no claim of its own: she came from the peoples Israel was told to drive out, and everything good in her came later, from the LORD. Verse 45 repeats the parentage.

a: rubbed with salt at all
p: Washing, rubbing with salt and wrapping were the care a newborn got. Jerusalem got none of it.
b: The verse lists what a midwife did: cut the cord, wash the baby, rub it with salt and wrap it in cloths. Rashi says salt was rubbed on a newborn 'so that his flesh hardens'. Greek and Roman writers also mention salt for newborns, but the custom is known to us mostly from this verse and from medieval comment on it. The point is not the medicine. The baby was treated as if no one wanted it.

a: You were dumped on the ground in a field
p: Abandoning an unwanted newborn is the picture. It was a real practice in the ancient world.
b: Exposing newborns, especially girls, was known in the ancient Mediterranean world. Ezekiel uses it as a parable and does not say that Jerusalem's parents did it. The phrase 'your life was loathed' (go'al nafshekh) says the child was despised from the first day. Notice that the child has no name, no father's care and no mother's. The only one who sees her is the LORD, who passes by in the next verse.

a: In your blood, live!
p: The LORD's word of life is spoken over a child still lying in her birth blood.
b: The MT has 'in your blood, live' twice. The Passover Haggadah quotes 16:6–7 in its account of Israel's growth in Egypt. Christian readers have heard a promise of life given before the child could earn it, as in Romans 5:6–8. Codex Vaticanus (as printed in Swete) has one short clause, 'from your blood, life', where the Hebrew has two commands to live; the repetition is gone, and 'in' has become 'from', so that life comes out of the blood instead of being spoken over the child lying in it.

a: reached the age for ornaments
p: The Hebrew says she came to ba'adi 'adayim, an odd phrase. It probably means the age of womanhood.
b: Ba'adi 'adayim is literally 'to the ornament of ornaments', and its meaning is not sure. The Plain follows the sense of the next clause (firm breasts, grown hair): the girl has come of age to wear jewelry and to marry. Codex Vaticanus has 'she came into cities of cities' (eis poleis poleon), which seems to read the Hebrew as 'arim, 'cities'. Some Hebrew manuscripts and modern commentators propose 'she came to full womanhood'. The reading of the Plain is the one most commentators take.

a: I spread the wing of my cloak over you
p: Spreading a garment over a woman was a sign of marriage and protection, as in Ruth 3:9.
b: In Ruth, Ruth asks Boaz: 'Spread the wing of your cloak over your servant' (Ruth 3:9). The same Hebrew word, kanaf, means 'wing' and 'corner of a garment'. To uncover a father's wing is a sexual wrong (Deuteronomy 22:30; 27:20). Here the LORD takes the role of husband. Codex Vaticanus also says 'wings' (pterygas).

a: came into a covenant with you
p: Ezekiel calls the LORD's bond with Israel a marriage covenant, as Hosea and Jeremiah did.
b: The prophets speak of the Sinai bond as a wedding: 'the love of your engagement' (Jeremiah 2:2; compare Hosea 2:14–20). Malachi 2:14 and Proverbs 2:17 call marriage itself a covenant. In the rabbis the giving of the Torah was Israel's wedding day (Mishnah Taanit 4:8). Notice that here the oath is sworn by the LORD, to a girl who has done nothing to deserve it. That sets up the shock of 16:59, where she has despised the oath.

a: fine leather
p: Tahash is a kind of leather that is also used on the tent of meeting, but no one knows the animal.
b: Tachash skins covered the tent of meeting (Exodus 25:5; 26:14; Numbers 4:6–14). English versions have 'badger' (KJV), 'sea cow', 'dolphin' and 'fine leather'. Some think the word is Egyptian, for a kind of leather. Ezekiel's list of finery for the bride (embroidered cloth, fine linen, tahash leather, silk) matches the materials of the tent of meeting, so the girl is dressed as a sanctuary. Codex Vaticanus has 'hyacinth-blue' (hyakinthon), as it does for the blue cloth of the tent.

a: silk
p: Meshi is found only here and in 16:13. 'Silk' is the old guess, and a good one.
b: Meshi appears only in 16:10 and 16:13 in the Hebrew Bible. 'Silk' has been the usual translation since the Middle Ages. Some scholars suggest instead 'fine gauze' or 'a sheer linen'. Codex Vaticanus has trichapton, 'fine hair-cloth'. The Plain keeps 'silk' as the traditional word.

a: Your fame went out among the nations because of your beauty
p: Jerusalem's beauty is also praised in the Psalms and in Lamentations.
b: Zion is called 'perfect in beauty' (Psalm 50:2) and 'beautiful in height' (Psalm 48:2). Lamentations 2:15 quotes the mockers asking whether this is 'the city that was called perfect in beauty'. The word for 'perfect' here is kalil, the same word Ezekiel uses of Tyre's beauty in 27:3 and 28:12. Ezekiel stresses that the splendor was 'what I had put on you': the beauty is a gift, not a possession.

a: acted as a prostitute
t: The marriage story and the criticism of it
p: Ezekiel 16 is one of the Bible's most disturbing chapters. Readers, ancient and modern, have asked what it does to those who hear it.
b: The image of Israel as an unfaithful wife begins with Hosea 1–3 and Jeremiah 2–3 and reaches its harshest form here and in Ezekiel 23. Defenders such as Greenberg and Block read the chapter as a prophet's deliberate shock, a story told to exiles who thought Jerusalem could never fall; Joyce surveys both sides. Feminist scholars, such as Setel, Weems, Darr and Galambush, ask what the story does to women who hear it, since the wife is shamed, stripped and killed while the husband is never judged. See the chapter page for the debate set out.

a: colorful high places
p: The 'high places' here are tents or booths hung with cloth. Women wove such hangings for the Asherah in Jerusalem.
b: A bamah is a shrine on a high place, but here it is made of the bride's own garments, so it is probably a booth or tent hung with colored cloth. 2 Kings 23:7 tells that in Josiah's reform women were weaving hangings for Asherah in the LORD's house. Codex Vaticanus has 'sewn idols' (eidola rhapta). The picture is of a girl who takes the clothes her husband gave her and uses them to build a place for another lover.

a: It was not to come, and it was never to be.
p: These words are a known puzzle. Some read them as a statement, and Codex Vaticanus reads them as a ban.
b: Lo ba'ot welo yihyeh is literally 'not coming, and it shall not be'. Commentators read it as the LORD's comment: 'such things should not happen and must not be' (the Plain), or as the reverse, 'it has never happened and never will' (as if she acted so wildly nothing like it had been). Codex Vaticanus reads it as a ban: 'you must not enter, and it must not happen'. The Hebrew text may also be damaged. The Plain keeps the form of a verdict.
orig: לֹא בָאוֹת וְלֹא יִהְיֶה (lo va'ot welo yihyeh)

a: male images
p: Tsalmei zakhar means 'male images', which may be statues of male gods or figures of the male body.
b: Tsalmei zakhar is 'images of a male'. Commentators understand statues of male deities (so Codex Vaticanus, eikonas arsenikas), or phallic figures. The Hebrew does not say which, and the Plain does not choose. Both readings fit the picture of the prostitute who makes models of her customers. The same word for 'image' is used of the figures of men painted on walls in 23:14.

a: as food
p: 'To be eaten' means the sacrifice is a meal, burned up as the god's food.
b: The infinitive le'ekhol, 'to eat', says the children were an offering that the images consumed. Codex Vaticanus has eis analosin, 'for consumption'. In Ezekiel's day the idea was that a sacrifice fed the god, which is why 16:19 says the bride set out food for the images and why God calls the food 'mine'. Ezekiel never says the idols ate anything. The point is that his gifts to Israel went to others.

a: making them pass over to the images
p: The verse says the children were given away and made to 'pass over'. The Hebrew has no word for fire here.
b: The verb is ha'avir, 'make pass over'. It is the verb used of giving children to Molech in Leviticus 18:21 and Jeremiah 32:35, and of making a son or daughter 'pass through the fire' in 2 Kings 23:10. Ezekiel himself says 'through the fire' only in 20:31; in 20:26 he uses the same verb of the firstborn, again without 'fire'. So the Plain says only what 16:21 says. 'Slaughtered' is the ordinary verb for killing a sacrificial animal. The children are called 'my' children and ones 'you bore to me', which treats them as the LORD's by right. Whether the Bible's child sacrifice reflects mass practice is debated; see the topic on Molech.
r: Leviticus 18:21; 2 Kings 23:10; Jeremiah 32:35; Ezekiel 20:26; Ezekiel 20:31; Ezekiel 23:37

a: a mound
p: Gev and ramah are rare words. Together they make a pun with bamah, the usual word for a high place.
b: Gev is found only in this chapter (16:24, 31, 39); it may mean a vaulted room, a mound or a platform. Ramah means 'height' (16:24, 25, 31, 39) and is close to bamah 'high place'. Codex Vaticanus takes it as 'a house for prostitution' (oikema pornikon), reading the whole as a brothel. The Plain uses 'mound' and 'high place' each time so a reader can follow the words.

a: You parted your legs
t: A plain phrase for an explicit one
p: The Hebrew says 'you opened wide your feet'. 'Feet' is a polite word in Hebrew for the legs and what lies between them.
b: Vattefasseqi et raglayikh is literally 'you spread open your feet'. Hebrew uses 'feet' as a gentle word for the body's private parts (compare Judges 3:24, 'cover his feet', and Isaiah 7:20, 'the hair of the feet'). Codex Vaticanus has 'you led your legs to every passer-by'. The Plain says 'parted your legs': it is as blunt as the Hebrew and adds nothing to it.

a: men of great flesh
p: The Hebrew is blunt about the Egyptians' virility. The Plain keeps a restrained form.
b: Gidlei basar is literally 'great of flesh'. It is a coarse way of speaking of the Egyptians' strength and appetite, matched by 23:20, where the lovers' 'flesh is the flesh of donkeys'. The historical referent is Judah's alliances with Egypt (Isaiah 30:1–5; 31:1–3; 2 Kings 17:4). Codex Vaticanus has megalosarkous, 'big in flesh'. The Plain neither softens nor adds to it.

a: I cut back your allotment
p: Choq can mean a portion of food or land. The LORD reduces what the bride was given.
b: Choq is a fixed share, whether of food (Proverbs 30:8) or a legal limit. The LORD cuts back her share as a punishment and lets the Philistine towns, her old enemies, set the price. 'Greed' translates nefesh, here the throat or appetite. Codex Vaticanus has 'souls' (psychas).

a: the Assyrians
p: Egypt, Assyria and Chaldea stand for Judah's foreign alliances over two centuries.
b: King Ahaz paid Tiglath-pileser of Assyria to rescue him from his neighbors (2 Kings 16:7–10); King Hezekiah showed his treasures to Merodach-baladan of Babylon (2 Kings 20:12–19) and later leaned on Egypt (Isaiah 30:1–7; 31:1). Ezekiel names the lovers in the order of Judah's history: Egypt, Assyria, then the Chaldeans (16:29). Each alliance brought a foreign god's altar with it (2 Kings 16:10–16). The picture is political and religious at once.

a: the land of traders, Chaldea
p: Kena'an means both 'Canaan' and 'trader'. Here it probably names Babylonia, the land of merchants.
b: Kena'an is the name Canaan, but it is also the ordinary word for a merchant (Zephaniah 1:11; Job 41:6). Babylonia was famous for trade, and Ezekiel calls it 'a land of traders' and 'a city of merchants' in 17:4. Codex Vaticanus keeps the proper name, reading 'toward the land of the Chaldeans' (pros gen Chaldaion). The Plain takes 'traders' because 'Chaldea' follows it and Judah's mother was already Canaanite (16:3).

a: How feeble is your heart
p: The Hebrew word 'amulah is found only here. Three readings have been proposed.
b: 'Amulah is not found elsewhere. It may come from a root meaning 'be weak or languish' (so 'how feeble is your heart', the Plain; the KJV has 'how weak'), or be a form meaning 'be filled with rage' ('how I burn with anger at you'). Codex Vaticanus takes it differently again: 'How shall I make [a covenant] with your daughter?' (ti diatho ten thygatera sou), which reads libbatekh 'your heart' as bittekh 'your daughter'. The Plain follows the first reading. The adjective shalleket 'headstrong' is also rare.

a: you looked down on the fee
p: A Dead Sea scroll preserves parts of 16:31 to 33 and agrees with the Masoretic Text.
b: The scroll 3QEzek (3Q1) has parts of 16:31–33, read here in the Abegg-Bowley-Cook transcription. It agrees with the Masoretic Text in every word that can be read. It spells 'you were' in 16:31 hyyty, as the Leningrad Codex writes the word (the Ketiv); the Qere, and the text as printed, read hyyt. In 16:31 the scroll's visible words include 'at the head of every road', 'in every public square', 'and you were not' and 'to scorn'; 'a prostitute' and 'payment' are restored by the editors. The verse says Jerusalem was worse than a prostitute: a prostitute at least takes a fee.

a: the reverse of other women
p: Jerusalem paid for her lovers. This matches Judah's tribute to Assyria and Babylon.
b: Hefekh means 'turning, reversal'. The nation 'paid the fee' to Assyria (2 Kings 16:8; 18:14–16), to Egypt and to Babylon, in silver and gold taken from the Temple. Hosea 8:9–10 says the same of Ephraim: 'Ephraim has hired lovers'. Codex Vaticanus has 'something twisted' (diestrammenon). The Plain keeps the plain sense: she did the opposite of every other prostitute.

a: your lust spilled out
p: Nechushtekh may mean 'your lust' or 'your copper' (money). Scholars still disagree.
b: Nechushtekh is built on nechoshet, which usually means 'copper' or 'bronze'. Codex Vaticanus has 'your bronze' (ton chalkon sou). Some think the word means money or metal poured out as payment. Others read it as a figure for her lust, and so do the Plain and the KJV ('filthiness'). The line then says she poured out her desire. Whichever is meant, the verse says her shame was seen.

a: filthy idols, your abhorrent things
p: Gillulim looks like a mocking word. It probably sounds like gelalim, 'dung pellets'.
b: Gillulim is Ezekiel's favorite word for idols (dozens of times). It resembles gelalim 'dung' and may be a deliberate insult, a play on the sound of galal, 'roll'. The Plain says 'filthy idols' each time, and keeps it apart from to'evot 'abhorrent things' and shiqqutsim 'detestable things'. Here the two words stand side by side: gillulei to'evotayikh, literally 'the idols of your abhorrent things', and the Plain gives each its own English. Codex Vaticanus has 'the thoughts of your lawless acts' (enthymemata ton anomion) and, in 18:6, 'the thoughts of the house of Israel', not 'idols'; in 18:12 it does say eidola.

a: the sentences given to women who commit adultery and shed blood
p: In Israel's law, a married woman and her lover were to be put to death. Ezekiel's list matches Leviticus 20:10.
b: Leviticus 20:10 and Deuteronomy 22:22 command death for both partners in adultery, and Deuteronomy 22:21 for a bride who deceives her husband. Stoning (16:40) is the law's penalty; the burning of her houses (16:41) is Ezekiel's own picture. The crowd and the 'many women' watching (16:41) make it a public judgment. 'Shed blood' joins it to the killing of children in 16:36. Ezekiel 23:45–47 repeats the sentence. The picture is a legal one, and it says nothing about what happened to real women in Israel's courts.

a: Like mother, like daughter.
p: Mashal is one Hebrew word with many English forms. Ezekiel uses it for a proverb, a riddle and a parable.
b: Mashal names a saying that compares: a proverb (16:44; 18:2–3), a parable or allegory (17:2; 24:3) or a taunt (Isaiah 14:4). The Plain says 'proverb' when the people quote a saying and 'parable' when Ezekiel tells a story. Here Ezekiel says that others will quote this saying against Jerusalem; Codex Vaticanus reads 'all they said against you in a parable'.

a: who live on your left hand
p: The Hebrew says 'on your left' and 'on your right'. Facing east, left is north and right is south.
b: The Hebrew says Samaria lives 'on your left' (al semolekh) and Sodom 'on your right'. Hebrew does have a word for north, tsafon, but this verse does not use it. Because Hebrew directions are given facing east, 'left' is north and 'right' is south; that is an interpretation of the orientation, and the Plain leaves the Hebrew words as they are. Codex Vaticanus also has 'left' and 'right'. Samaria lies to Jerusalem's north, and Sodom, in the Hebrew Bible's geography, lies to the south, near the Dead Sea. 'Older' and 'younger' translate gedolah and qetannah, which also mean 'greater' and 'smaller': Samaria was the larger kingdom.

a: pride, a full belly of food, and easy, quiet comfort
t: The sin of Sodom, as Ezekiel names it
p: Ezekiel lists Sodom's guilt as pride, plenty and ignoring the poor. Other books name other wrongs. Readers differ on how they fit.
b: Ezekiel names pride, a surplus of food, a comfortable life and refusing to help the poor and needy, followed in 16:50 by 'something abhorrent' (to'evah). Genesis 19:4–9 shows a mob demanding to abuse the guests, and Isaiah 1:10 and Jeremiah 23:14 call Jerusalem's leaders 'Sodom' for their injustice and lies. Wisdom 19:13–15 stresses inhospitality, Jude 7 sexual wrong, and Jewish tradition cruelty to the stranger: 'What is mine is mine and what is yours is yours' is the character of Sodom (Mishnah Avot 5:10; Babylonian Talmud, Sanhedrin 109a). Some commentators hear in 'something abhorrent' the word used in Leviticus 18:22; others say Ezekiel's list comes first, and the abuse of guests in Genesis 19 was an act of the same pride. The Plain gives the list as written.
r: Genesis 19:4–9; Isaiah 1:10; Jeremiah 23:14; Wisdom 19:13–15; Jude 7; Leviticus 18:22

a: something abhorrent
p: To'evah is singular here. It names one act, and the verse does not say which.
b: Verse 50 says 'something abhorrent' (singular), while the chapter's other uses are plural. The Hebrew does not say what the act was. The same word is used of idolatry, child sacrifice, dishonest scales (Proverbs 11:1) and sexual wrongs (Leviticus 18:22–30). So a reader must decide from context, which is why churches and commentators differ; see the note at 16:49. 'As soon as I saw it' (ka'asher ra'iti) points back to Genesis 18:21, where the LORD goes down 'to see'.

a: made your sisters' case look better
p: Jerusalem's sins were so bad that Sodom and Samaria look innocent beside her.
b: Pillalt means 'you mediated, you pleaded' (1 Samuel 2:25). By sinning worse, Jerusalem has become her sisters' defense lawyer: her record makes theirs look righteous. Ezekiel does not say Samaria and Sodom were innocent. He says they were less guilty. The point is the shame of being outdone by those you called wicked.

a: I will turn their fortunes around
p: The promise includes Sodom. Readers have taken this as a real restoration, as irony or as a pointed insult to Jerusalem.
b: Shuv shevut is the phrase for 'restoring fortunes' (Jeremiah 29:14; 30:3; 32:44). The Ketiv derives the noun from shevi 'captivity', while the Qere reads shevut; Codex Vaticanus has 'I will turn their turning'. Sodom was destroyed and could not be restored in the ordinary sense, so some take the promise as hyperbole, an insult meant to shame Jerusalem ('even Sodom will get back what she had'), or a promise that even the worst will be included in God's final mercy. Commentators read it each way. The Plain keeps the promise to Sodom, because the Hebrew gives it.

a: an everlasting covenant
t: The covenant that is not undone
p: The promise recalls the covenants with Noah, Abraham and David and points ahead to Jeremiah's new covenant.
b: 'Everlasting covenant' (berit olam) is used of Noah (Genesis 9:16), Abraham (Genesis 17:7) and David (2 Samuel 23:5). Jeremiah promises one in 32:40 and 50:5, and Ezekiel again in 37:26. Compare the 'new covenant' of Jeremiah 31:31–34. In Ezekiel the new bond is the LORD's act alone: he remembers, he establishes, he atones. Whether it is the same as the new covenant of Jeremiah, and how Christians relate it to the church, are old questions; see the topic on the covenant.
r: Genesis 9:16; Genesis 17:7; 2 Samuel 23:5; Jeremiah 32:40; Jeremiah 50:5; Ezekiel 37:26

a: though not through your covenant
p: The sisters will be given to Jerusalem as daughters, but not under the old agreement.
b: Mibberitekh can mean 'not out of your covenant' (not because of the Sinai covenant that Jerusalem broke), 'not by your doing', or 'not as part of your covenant'. Codex Vaticanus has ouk ek diathekes sou, 'not from your covenant'. The usual reading is that Samaria and Sodom come to Jerusalem by grace and not by any right under the old agreement. The Plain keeps the wording open.

a: when I atone for you
p: Here God himself is the one who covers the guilt. No sacrifice is named.
b: Kipper is the Bible's verb for covering guilt, as on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16). Usually the priest is the subject. Here and in Psalm 65:3, Psalm 78:38 and Deuteronomy 21:8 the LORD acts alone. Codex Vaticanus has en to exilaskesthai me soi 'when I am merciful to you'. The result is not pride but silence: she will never open her mouth because of her disgrace.

a: tell a riddle and speak a parable
p: Ezekiel calls this a riddle and a parable. Unlike most riddles, it comes with its answer.
b: Chidah is a riddle, such as Samson's (Judges 14:12–14). Mashal is a parable. Codex Vaticanus has diegema 'story' and parabole 'parable'. What is unusual is that 17:11–21 gives the answer at once, which tells us how close the exiles were to missing the point: they needed it spelled out. Verses 22–24 then go beyond the riddle to a promise.

a: The great eagle came to Lebanon
t: The two eagles and the cedar
p: The first eagle is the king of Babylon. The cedar is the royal house of David.
b: Verse 12 names the first eagle: Nebuchadnezzar. The Bible elsewhere compares Babylon's army to an eagle (Jeremiah 48:40; 49:22; Habakkuk 1:8). The cedar of Lebanon stands for the royal house of David, whose palace was built of cedar (1 Kings 7:2; Jeremiah 22:6–7, 23). 'The top of a cedar' is King Jehoiachin, taken to Babylon in 597 BC. The second eagle is Pharaoh (17:15, 17). Notice that Ezekiel does not condemn Babylon here: the eagle's coming is the LORD's act, and Zedekiah's revolt is the sin.

a: a land of traders
p: Kena'an means 'trader' as well as 'Canaan'. It is Babylon, as the next phrase 'a city of merchants' shows.
b: Both kena'an and rokhlim ('merchants') belong to the language of trade. Codex Vaticanus has gen Chanaan, 'land of Canaan', and then 'a walled city' (polin teteichismenen), where the Hebrew has 'a city of merchants'. The Plain takes the Hebrew as describing Babylon, as in 16:29. The shoot carried to Babylon is Jehoiachin, who was deported with his officials in 597 BC (2 Kings 24:12–15).

a: the way one plants a willow
p: Tsaftsafah occurs only here. 'Willow' is an old guess based on Arabic.
b: Tsaftsafah is found only here. 'Willow' follows the Arabic safsaf and later Jewish tradition. Other suggestions include a word meaning 'to be set as a marker' or a kind of plant growing by water. Codex Vaticanus has 'looking out' (epiblepomenon), a different reading. 'It took one of the seed of the land' means a native plant, here Zedekiah, a son of Josiah and uncle of Jehoiachin (2 Kings 24:17).

a: became a vine
p: A vine spreading low is a small, dependent kingdom, not a mighty tree.
b: Israel is often a vine (Psalm 80:8–16; Isaiah 5:1–7; Hosea 10:1) and in Ezekiel 15 the vine is useless wood. Here the vine is 'low of stature'. It spreads, but cannot stand alone; its branches turn to the eagle and its roots are 'under him'. Verse 14 says what the low vine means: a lowly kingdom that does not exalt itself and keeps its covenant. That was Zedekiah's place, a vassal of Babylon.

a: another great eagle
p: The second eagle is Egypt's king. Zedekiah turned to him when Babylon pressed.
b: 2 Kings 24:20 says Zedekiah rebelled against the king of Babylon, and 2 Chronicles 36:13 adds that the king had sworn an oath by God. The Pharaoh of the revolt is usually taken as Hophra (Apries, 589–570 BC), named in Jeremiah 44:30, who marched to relieve Jerusalem and was turned back (Jeremiah 37:5–11). Some date the intrigues earlier, to the visit of Psammetichus II to Palestine in 592 or 591 BC, close to the date of the surrounding chapters; reported by commentaries, and not settled. Jeremiah 27:1–3 also records envoys from neighboring kings meeting Zedekiah.

a: Will he not tear out its roots
p: The Hebrew does not name the one who pulls up the vine. It could be the LORD, the first eagle or any 'he'.
b: The Hebrew verb is 'he will pull up', with no named subject. Commentators think of the LORD (as in 17:20), of the first eagle, or of an unnamed attacker. The Plain leaves it as 'he'. Codex Vaticanus has a passive: 'the roots of its tenderness and its fruit will rot'. The last line says it will not take 'a strong arm or many people' to do it, which is unusual for a conquest and is meant to say: the LORD's decision is enough.

a: the east wind
p: The qadim is the hot desert wind. In the Bible it often stands for God's judgment.
b: Qadim is the dry wind from the desert that withers plants (Hosea 13:15; Jonah 4:8; Genesis 41:6). In Exodus 14:21 the LORD drives back the sea with it. Ezekiel uses it again in 19:12 and 27:26. It is not named as Babylon; it is God's judgment. Codex Vaticanus has kauson, 'scorching wind'.

a: rebellious house
p: This is Ezekiel's name for the people. The Plain uses it each time.
b: Beit meri is 'rebellious house'. It first appears in 2:5–8 and then in 3:9, 26–27; 12:2–3; 24:3 and 44:6. The Plain keeps one English phrase so a reader can follow it. Codex Vaticanus says oikos parapikrainon 'embittering house'. Here the rebels are asked a question they ought to be able to answer: 'Do you not know what these things mean?'

a: the powerful men of the land
p: Nebuchadnezzar took Jehoiachin, his officials and the leading men of Judah, and put Zedekiah on the throne.
b: 2 Kings 24:12–17 tells how the king of Babylon 'took away' Jehoiachin and 'the powerful men of the land' (2 Kings 24:15) and made Mattaniah, Jehoiachin's uncle, king under the name Zedekiah. A treaty with an oath was the usual way to bind a vassal. Ezekiel was among those taken (1:1–2). The Hebrew 'elei ha'arets is literally 'the rams of the land'. The Plain uses 'powerful men' as in 2 Kings 24:15.

a: sent envoys to Egypt
p: Zedekiah sent envoys to Egypt for horses and an army. Jeremiah told him not to.
b: Judah had few horses; Egypt was famous for them (Isaiah 31:1; Deuteronomy 17:16). Jeremiah and Ezekiel both counted the alliance as a breach of Zedekiah's oath to Babylon (Jeremiah 27:12–15; 37:5–10). Isaiah had warned Hezekiah against the same thing (Isaiah 30:1–7). The questions 'Will he prosper? Will he escape?' expect the answer no. Codex Vaticanus reads: 'he will fall away from him by sending his messengers to Egypt'.

a: will do anything for him in the war
p: Pharaoh's army did come out, and Babylon briefly left Jerusalem. Then the siege resumed.
b: Jeremiah 37:5–11 tells that Pharaoh's army marched and the Chaldeans lifted the siege for a short time, and that Jeremiah warned they would come back. A ramp piled up and a siege wall built is what the siege of Jerusalem was (2 Kings 25:1; Jeremiah 52:4). Ezekiel's word was spoken before this, if the oracle is dated to about 591 BC; if the events of 17:15 are the later embassy, he is describing a coming failure.

a: the oath he despised is my oath
t: An oath to Babylon that is the LORD's
p: Ezekiel counts Zedekiah's oath to the king of Babylon as an oath sworn to the LORD.
b: 2 Chronicles 36:13 says Nebuchadnezzar made Zedekiah swear 'by God'. Ezekiel therefore calls the broken treaty 'my oath' and 'my covenant', so that rebellion against Babylon is treason against the LORD. This shows how seriously Israel took an oath, as with the Gibeonites (Joshua 9:19–20; 2 Samuel 21:1–2). It is also a hard saying for those who see Babylon as an empire to be resisted, and Jeremiah's counsel to submit in 27:12–15 is the same. Whether Ezekiel is supporting Babylon, or only saying that an oath to God is not to be played with, is discussed by commentators.

a: I will throw my net over him
p: Ezekiel says the same of the king in 12:13. Zedekiah was caught near Jericho, blinded and taken to Babylon.
b: In 12:13 the LORD says: he will bring the king to Babylon, where he will die yet not see it. 2 Kings 25:4–7 tells that Zedekiah fled by night, was caught on the plains of Jericho, saw his sons killed, and was blinded; Jeremiah 52:11 says he was kept in prison until his death. The verse is often used to show how Ezekiel's words were fulfilled. Whether 12:13 and 17:20 were spoken before the event or sharpened after it is a question between traditional and critical readers.

a: his fugitives among all his troops
p: Commentators think 'fugitives' may stand for 'choice troops', since fugitives do not make up an army.
b: Mivrachav means 'his fugitives'; the Masoretic notes record only a spelling difference (Ketiv/Qere) in the word. Because fugitives would not be 'among his troops' and fall by the sword, commentators have suggested changing one letter to mivcharav, 'his choice ones'. Codex Vaticanus has 'in all his battle line' (en pase parataxei autou). The Plain keeps the Hebrew.

a: a shoot from the high crown of the cedar
p: The ancient readers took this as a promise of a king of David's line. They did not agree on which king.
b: The Targum of Jonathan says the LORD will 'bring near from the kingdom of the house of David, compared to a tall cedar' a 'tender one from the sons of his sons' who will become 'a mighty king' (read on Sefaria, English as given there). Rashi adds: 'And I Myself will take: the King Messiah'. Radak reads it of Zerubbabel, grandson of Jehoiachin, whom he names (Hebrew text on Sefaria). Christian writers have taken it as Christ, and the birds that nest in the shade are echoed in Jesus' parable of the mustard seed (Mark 4:30–32). A critical view says it is simply a promise that the line of David will be re-planted. Compare Isaiah 11:1, Jeremiah 23:5 and Ezekiel 34:23–24, which use other words.
r: Isaiah 11:1; Jeremiah 23:5; Ezekiel 34:23–24; Ezekiel 37:24; Mark 4:30–32; Zechariah 6:12

a: Birds of every wing will live under it
p: The tree that shelters every bird is also in Ezekiel 31:6, Daniel 4:12 and the Gospels.
b: Ezekiel 31:6 uses the same picture of Assyria as a cedar, and Daniel 4:12, 21 of Nebuchadnezzar's tree. In Mark 4:32 and Matthew 13:32 Jesus says the mustard plant grows large enough for 'the birds of the sky to nest in its shade'. In Ezekiel the birds may stand for the nations that come to a restored kingdom. Codex Vaticanus has 'every bird and every winged thing'.

a: I bring the tall tree low and raise the low tree up
p: The LORD brings down the high and lifts the low. Hannah and Mary sing the same.
b: This is a recurring theme: Hannah's song (1 Samuel 2:7–8), Isaiah 2:12–17, and Mary's Magnificat (Luke 1:52). The verb is hishpalti, 'I bring low', not 'I cut down': the Hebrew has the tall tree humbled, not felled. The 'trees of the field' are the nations, who will know that the LORD, not Babylon or Egypt, decided Judah's fate. The closing we'asiti, 'and I will act', sets his word over the plans of kings.

a: The fathers ate sour grapes
p: Jeremiah quotes this saying too, and Lamentations 5:7 voices the feeling behind it.
b: Jeremiah 31:29–30 quotes the proverb and promises that it will stop: 'The fathers ate sour grapes, and the children's teeth go numb' (Jeremiah 31:29). Jeremiah says it in the future of the new covenant; Ezekiel says it now, as a call to turn. Lamentations 5:7 is the people's complaint of the same kind: 'Our ancestors sinned, and they are gone; we are the ones who carry their guilt' (Lamentations 5:7). The saying fits the exiles' belief that Manasseh's sins (2 Kings 21:10–15; 23:26–27) had already decided their fate.

a: go numb
p: Qahah means to be dull or blunt, as when teeth lose feeling from sour fruit.
b: Qahah means 'be dull, blunt'. The KJV and many versions say 'set on edge', which is the feeling most people know from sour fruit. The Hebrew of the saying is the same as in Jeremiah 31:29 word for word, and the Plain gives it the same English there and here, including 'ate'. The verb yokhelu is a form that can be past or present, and 'you keep reciting' in Ezekiel would also allow 'eat'; the Plain keeps Jeremiah's 'ate' so that the two books quote one saying. Codex Vaticanus also has a past tense, 'the fathers ate sour grapes' (ephagon), and 'were set on edge' (egomphiasan).

a: The person who sins, that very person will die.
p: Nefesh is 'life' or 'person'. The old 'the soul that sins will die' has been used for debates the verse is not about.
b: The KJV has 'the soul that sinneth, it shall die', which is a literal rendering of nefesh. In Hebrew nefesh is a living being, a person or a life, not a separate part that survives the body. Some Christian groups that teach the soul does not survive death cite this verse for that; others answer that 'die' here means the judgment of the wicked, not the nature of the soul. The Plain says 'person'. The verse is a rule of justice: each answers for his own sin. Compare 18:20.
orig: הַנֶּפֶשׁ הַחֹטֵאת הִיא תָמוּת (hanefesh hachote hi tamut)

a: on the mountains
p: Eating 'on the mountains' probably means the sacrificial meals at high-place shrines.
b: The Hebrew says only el heharim, 'on the mountains' (here and in 18:11, 15; 22:9). It is usually taken to mean the sacrificial meals at the high places, where the shared meat of the offering was eaten before the idol (compare 1 Corinthians 10:20–21); the Plain does not add the word 'shrines'. Codex Vaticanus is the same: epi ton oreon ouk phagetai. The list that follows (idols, a neighbor's wife, a woman during her period) is sometimes compared with the entrance questions of Psalm 15 and Psalm 24:3–6. Job 31 swears the same kind of oath of innocence.

a: monthly uncleanness
p: Intercourse during a woman's period is forbidden in Leviticus.
b: Niddah names the impurity of a woman's monthly flow (Leviticus 15:19–24). Leviticus 18:19 and 20:18 forbid sexual relations with her during it. Ezekiel mentions the rule in his list of a just man's habits because he, a priest, reads the law as a whole: worship, sex and money are all questions of justice. In 22:10 he lists breaking the same rule among Jerusalem's crimes.

a: the pledge a debtor gave him
p: A poor man's cloak given as a pledge had to be given back before night.
b: Exodus 22:26–27 and Deuteronomy 24:12–13 require that a cloak taken as a pledge be returned by sunset, because it is the poor man's only cover. Amos 2:8 condemns those who lie down on garments taken in pledge. Ezekiel 18:7, 12, 16 repeat the rule three times in this chapter. Compare also Job 22:6 and Job 24:9. The Plain uses 'pledge' every time, as in these laws.

a: makes no loan at interest and takes no profit
p: Two words, neshekh and tarbit, are in the laws against lending at interest to a fellow Israelite.
b: The law forbids charging an Israelite interest: 'Do not charge your brother interest' (Deuteronomy 23:19; see also Exodus 22:25 and Leviticus 25:36–37). Neshekh (a 'bite') is interest; tarbit (or marbit) is increase, a profit. Ezekiel lists it among the sins of a lender (18:13, 17; 22:12). Later Christian debates about 'usury' often cite these laws (see the topic on interest and debt). Whether the law bans all interest or only the exploiting of the poor is discussed by commentators.

a: He will certainly live, the Lord GOD declares.
p: In this chapter 'live' and 'die' first mean surviving or perishing in the coming disaster. Later readers have heard more.
b: The Hebrew doubles the verb (chayoh yichyeh, 'living he will live'). In Ezekiel, life is the opposite of death in the judgment on Jerusalem (3:21; 33:15–16). The offer to the exile is to live in the land, in the LORD's favor. Later Jewish and Christian readers heard also the life of the age to come. Which of these Ezekiel meant is discussed. The Plain keeps the plain word 'live'.

a: does any one of these things,
p: The Hebrew has an odd word, 'ach, here. It may mean 'alas', 'a brother' or be a slip.
b: The Hebrew line is we'asah ach me'achad me'elleh. The word 'ach may be 'a brother' (so the sense 'does to a brother any one of these things'), an exclamation 'alas', or a copying slip. Codex Vaticanus leaves it out and says only that he 'sheds blood and commits a sin'. The Plain reads 'any one of these things' and leaves the odd word untranslated.

a: though he himself did none of these things
p: The Hebrew says only 'and he, all these things he did not do'. Readers differ on whether 'he' is the father or the son.
b: Ve-hu et kol elleh lo asah has the pronoun hu, 'he', and names no one. Many English versions and Block take it as the father of 18:10: the son does these sins 'though' his father did none of them. Codex Vaticanus takes the son as the subject: 'he did not walk in the way of his righteous father'. Those are opposite referents, and the Hebrew does not decide. The Plain keeps 'he himself' and, in the next sentence, calls the one who has eaten on the mountains 'that son', which both readings allow. See the variant at this verse.
orig: וְהוּא אֶת־כָּל־אֵלֶּה לֹא עָשָׂה (ve-hu et kol elleh lo asah)

a: A son will not bear the guilt of his father
p: Moses spoke of guilt reaching children; Deuteronomy bars killing children for fathers. How does Ezekiel fit?
b: Exodus 20:5 says the LORD brings 'the fathers' guilt home to the children' (Exodus 20:5), and Deuteronomy 24:16 says 'children must not be put to death because of their fathers' (Deuteronomy 24:16). 2 Kings 14:6 applies that law to King Amaziah. In the Talmud, Makkot 24a has Moses say 'He visits the transgression of the fathers upon the sons' (Exodus 34:7) and Ezekiel come and revoke it with 'The soul that sins, it shall die' (as read on Sefaria in English). A way of fitting the verses together is given in Berakhot 7a, which sets Exodus 34:7 against Deuteronomy 24:16, cites Exodus 20:5 ('those who hate me') in the answer, and divides the cases between children who adopt their ancestors' actions and children who do not; that passage does not mention Ezekiel. Kaminsky argues that the idea was not new with Ezekiel and that Ezekiel does not wipe out all shared responsibility; Greenberg reads the chapter as an answer to the exiles' fatalism. The old critical claim that Ezekiel 'invented' individual responsibility is contested. Notice that 18:20 is about a court and about blame, and does not say that no one ever suffers for another's sin: see the chapter page.

a: Is it the death of the wicked that I really take pleasure in
t: God's pleasure and the death of the wicked
p: God asks whether he wants anyone to die. The same words come back in 33:11 and in the New Testament.
b: The question expects the answer no, and the verse returns in 18:32 and 33:11. 1 Timothy 2:4 says God wants all people to be saved, and 2 Peter 3:9 says he is patient and does not want anyone to perish; Christians have linked these to this verse. How this fits with election and predestination is a question on which churches differ: see the card at 18:32.

a: The Lord's way is not fair
p: Lo yittakhen means 'is not weighed rightly'. It is the accusation that God's justice is crooked.
b: Tikken is 'to weigh, measure, set straight'. The people say the Lord's way is not evenly weighed. Ezekiel repeats the charge in 18:29 and 33:17, 20. Abraham asked, 'Will the Judge of all the earth not do what is just?' (Genesis 18:25); Malachi 2:17 and Job make similar complaints. Codex Vaticanus has ou kateuthynei, 'does not go straight'. The LORD answers by turning the charge around: it is the people's ways that are not straight.

a: Turn back! Turn away from all your rebellious acts
p: Shuv is both 'turn back' (return) and 'turn away from' (leave). Ezekiel's one verb is rendered by its construction in this chapter.
b: Shuv appears in 18:21, 23, 24, 26, 27, 28, 30, 32. The Plain follows one rule. When the verb is followed by 'from' (min), whether the thing left is sin or righteousness, it is 'turn away from' (18:21, 23, 24, 26, 27, 28 and the second verb of 18:30). When it stands alone as a call to return, it is 'turn back' (the first verb of 18:30, and 18:32). Jeremiah makes a famous play on the same verb (Jeremiah 3:12–14, 22).

a: Make yourselves a new heart and a new spirit
p: Here the people are told to make themselves a new heart. In 36:26 the LORD says he will give it.
b: Ezekiel 36:26 says, 'I will give you a new heart', and 11:19 has the same promise. Here the people are commanded to make one. Deuteronomy puts both side by side: 'circumcise your hearts' (Deuteronomy 10:16) and 'the LORD your God will circumcise your heart' (Deuteronomy 30:6). Augustine prayed 'Give what you command, and command what you will' (Confessions 10.29), and used such verses against Pelagius, who held that a command implies the ability to obey. Reformed readers hear in the command the way God works grace; Wesleyan readers hear a real call to a free response. Jewish readers have seen repentance as always within reach (Deuteronomy 30:11–14). The Plain keeps the command.

a: I take no pleasure in the death of anyone who dies
p: The chapter ends on God's wish: 'turn back and live'.
b: The verse repeats 18:23 and brings the chapter to a call. The call 'turn back and live' echoes Deuteronomy 30:19 'choose life'. See the card on this page for how churches read God's desire for all to live alongside election.

a: the leaders of Israel
p: Nasi' is the title Ezekiel uses for the rulers of Judah, including the kings, and avoids the word 'king'.
b: Nasi' is 'leader' (it is the Plain's word for it everywhere). The KJV and many versions say 'prince'. Ezekiel prefers it to 'king' for Judah's rulers (as in 7:27; 12:10; 21:25). Codex Vaticanus has the singular, 'the ruler of Israel' (ton archonta tou Israel), which is a variant. The poem names no one, and it is a matter of dispute which kings are meant.

a: sing a lament
p: Qinah is the song for the dead. Ezekiel sings several, for Judah's kings and for Tyre and Egypt.
b: The qinah is a funeral lament, usually in a limping rhythm of a long line followed by a short one. David sang one for Saul and Jonathan (2 Samuel 1:17–27), and Amos 5:1 uses the form for Israel. Ezekiel sings laments for Tyre (26:17; 27:2; 28:12) and for Pharaoh (32:2). This one is sung for people who are not yet dead: the kings of Judah, two of them already in chains.

a: What was your mother? A lioness!
p: The mother is Judah or Jerusalem. The lion is the royal animal of Judah.
b: Jacob's blessing calls Judah 'a lion's cub' (Genesis 49:9), and the lion is the emblem of Judah's kings. Some commentators take the lioness as the nation of Judah, others as the city of Jerusalem, and some, because of 2 Kings 23:31 and 24:18, as Hamutal, the mother of both Jehoahaz and Zedekiah. The poem does not say. 'Your mother' speaks to the leaders of 19:1 as her cubs. The Targum, as read on Sefaria, calls the lioness 'the Congregation of Israel' (and so the vine of 19:10), with the cubs as kings. Rashi, in the Judaica Press translation on Sefaria, also gives 'the congregation of Israel' for the mother (on 19:5) and takes the cubs as sons of Josiah. Codex Vaticanus has 'what was your mother? A cub'.

a: with hooks they led him
t: The first cub goes to Egypt
p: The first cub is most likely King Jehoahaz, taken to Egypt by Pharaoh Neco in 609 BC.
b: 2 Kings 23:31–34 says that Jehoahaz reigned three months, that Pharaoh Neco locked him up at Riblah, and that 'Jehoahaz came to Egypt and died there' (2 Kings 23:34). The hooks (in the nose or jaw) are the way captive animals and kings were led; compare 2 Kings 19:28 and Ezekiel 29:4; 38:4. Whether the poem means exactly him is debated, since the cub 'learned to tear prey' (19:3), which suits a longer reign. The poem may be a type of each ruler's fall, not a record of one.

a: she took another of her cubs
p: Commentators name Jehoiachin or Zedekiah; some propose Jehoiakim. The Hebrew says 'one of her cubs', as in 19:3.
b: The Hebrew says echad, 'one', of her cubs, the same word as in 19:3 ('One of her cubs'); the Plain says 'another' because it is a second cub, and Codex Vaticanus has allon, 'another'. The second cub grows to roar, lays waste cities and is taken to Babylon in a cage (19:9). Jehoiachin was taken to Babylon after three months in 597 BC (2 Kings 24:8–15), and 19:9 can be read with that. Zedekiah was taken to Babylon after his capture (2 Kings 25:6–7), and the 'net' and 'pit' echo 12:13 and 17:20. Jehoiakim, who was bound to be taken to Babylon according to 2 Chronicles 36:6, has also been proposed, and Rashi (as read on Sefaria) names Jehoiakim for the second cub and Jehoahaz for the first. If the second cub is Zedekiah, the poem cannot have been spoken in 592 to 591 BC. The poem's lack of names leaves it open.

a: He knew his widows
p: The Hebrew says the lion 'knew his widows'. It is a hard text, and the Plain translates it closely and does not smooth it.
b: Vayyeda' almenotav is literally 'and he knew his widows'. Two things are odd. The verb yada', 'know', is the Bible's word for sexual knowledge as well as for knowing (Genesis 4:1), and Rashi (Judaica Press translation on Sefaria) takes it so: the lion 'was intimate with their widows', which he explains as raping the women and killing their husbands. And the suffix is 'his', while the next line says 'their cities'. For these reasons many commentators change one letter and read armenotav, 'his palaces' or 'strongholds', which suits 'laid waste their cities'; the Targum (as read on Sefaria) has 'he laid waste their palaces'. Codex Vaticanus has neither: 'he ranged in his boldness'. No Hebrew manuscript is cited here for the change. The Plain keeps the Hebrew words and does not choose among the senses; see the variant.

a: took him to the king of Babylon
p: Babylonian ration tablets list 'Ya'ukin, king of Judah' and his sons.
b: Tablets found in Babylon, from the reign of Nebuchadnezzar, list oil rations for 'Ya'ukin, king of Judah' and his sons (first published by Weidner in 1939; reported here from Cogan and Tadmor's commentary on 2 Kings). 2 Kings 25:27–30 tells how Evil-merodach later released Jehoiachin from prison. If the second cub is Jehoiachin, 'his voice would not be heard again on the mountains of Israel' is the lament's verdict on a king who never returned.

a: like a vine in your blood
p: The Hebrew says 'in your blood', which makes little picture of a vine. The text may be damaged.
b: Kaggefen bedamkha is literally 'like a vine in your blood'. The same word dam, 'blood', is in 16:6 and 16:22, but nothing in the poem is about blood, and 'planted beside water' follows at once. Codex Vaticanus has hos ampelos kai hos anthos en rhoa, 'like a vine and like a flower in a pomegranate', which seems to read a different Hebrew word. Commentators have proposed other changes, such as 'in your vineyard' or 'in your likeness'. The Plain keeps the Hebrew words so that a reader can see that the verse is hard. See the variant. The 'mother' is the lioness of 19:2, now a vine.

a: made to be rulers' scepters
p: The vine's branches are the royal line, fit to be a ruler's staff.
b: The word for 'branch' (mateh) is also a staff, and a ruler's staff is a scepter. The strong branches are the kings of David's house. Genesis 49:10 says the scepter will not depart from Judah. The lament is that the vine, once so tall that it was seen from afar, is now uprooted and burned, and 19:14 ends with 'no scepter to rule'. Compare the vine of 17:6 and the vine of Psalm 80.

a: They were torn off and dried up, her strong branch
p: The verbs are plural ('they were torn off and dried up') and the branch is singular. The Plain keeps the mismatch.
b: Hitparequ vayyavesh matteh uzzah has a plural verb ('they were torn off') followed by a singular noun, 'the branch of her strength'. Commentators take the singular as a collective for the strong branches of 19:11, or think the text has been disturbed. The Plain keeps the order of the Hebrew and leaves 'they' for the reader to join to the branches. The wind that dries the fruit is the same qadim as in 17:10.
orig: הִתְפָּרְקוּ וַיִּבָשׁו מַטֵּה עִזָּה (hitparequ vayyavesh matteh uzzah)

a: It is a lament, and it has become a lament.
p: The last line may be Ezekiel's remark: this is a lament, and it has become one.
b: Qinah hi wattehi leqinah is literally 'a lament it is, and it became a lament'. It may be the prophet's comment on the poem (it is a lament, and so it was used as one), or a statement that what is said has come true: the lament has become a real one. The verb can be read as past ('has become') or as a future ('will become'). Codex Vaticanus has 'a tribe is in a parable of lament, and will become a lament'. The Plain keeps the plain Hebrew.
orig: קִינָה הִיא וַתְּהִי לְקִינָה (qinah hi wattehi leqinah)
